# Diagnosing the 2009 Buick Enclave No-Start: Beyond the Timing Chain

A 2009 Buick Enclave with a 3.6L V6 engine presenting a no-start condition often triggers immediate suspicion of timing chain failure, especially after recent mechanical intervention. This specific case involves an engine that has undergone multiple timing chain replacements, resulting in intermittent stalling and a persistent P0336 code. The vehicle was recently repaired by a third party who replaced the crankshaft position sensor (CKP) but failed to resolve the underlying issue. Complicating the diagnosis is significant compression loss: cylinders 1 and 3 are reading approximately 115 psi and 75 psi respectively, against an average of 175 psi on the other cylinders.

Before diving into oscilloscope analysis, it is crucial to address the mechanical reality of that compression discrepancy. While the stored code points to sensor performance, a drop from 175 psi to 75 psi in a single cylinder suggests a catastrophic failure within the combustion chamber or valvetrain. Common culprits include a blown head gasket, a broken valve spring, or a bent valve. The fact that the cylinder heads were previously removed for "unclear reasons" raises red flags regarding potential warping or improper re-torquing of head bolts. Low battery voltage can also skew compression readings and confuse ignition timing strategies, so ensuring adequate cranking speed is a prerequisite for any valid diagnostic data.

The diagnostic approach shifted to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) once mechanical access was limited. With the PCM located on the upper radiator support, backprobing the Bank 1 intake camshaft position sensor (CMP) and the CKP signal wires provided a window into the engine's timing logic. The captured waveform showed consistent signals without dropouts, and the CKP Resync PID indicated active counts. This data initially contradicted the P0336 code, suggesting the PCM is receiving valid pulses but perhaps struggling to synchronize them due to physical timing errors or voltage instability.

A critical observation during this analysis was the noise on the low reference circuit during initial turn-over, measuring less than 0.5V of deviation. In a noisy electrical environment, such as a shop with heavy machinery or alternators spinning up, ground bounce can cause sensor signals to fluctuate. While 0.5V seems minor, it is sufficient to disrupt the precise timing calculations required for direct injection and variable valve timing systems. The fuel rail pressure sensor reading of .5 mPa matches the expected state at idle or no-start conditions, ruling out a major fuel delivery failure as the primary cause.

It is important to note that without capturing Bank 2 CMP sensors and an exhaust camshaft sensor in the same capture, establishing a definitive correlation between all four cams and the crank is impossible. A missing correlation window might hide a phase shift where one cam is late while others are on time. Furthermore, comparing these waveforms against a known-good reference or performing a dynamic backfire test (if safe) would help isolate whether the P0336 is a true sensor fault or a mechanical timing offset caused by the repeated chain work.

The compression issue remains the most pressing hardware failure. If cylinder 3 has 75 psi, the engine will not run smoothly regardless of how perfect the CKP signal is. The PCM may enter a limp mode or refuse to fire injectors if it detects inconsistent compression ratios over multiple cycles. Addressing the mechanical integrity of cylinders 1 and 3âlikely via head gasket repair or valve replacementâis mandatory before returning the vehicle to service.
